title: Economic Importance of Bacteria and Fungi
tagline: What bacteria do for and against us, and the ways fungi are used to make bread, medicine and food.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every organism, process and application below is standard microbiology, and the scope follows the registered blurb: the useful and harmful roles of bacteria and the useful role of fungi. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Bacteria and fungi are the two groups of microorganisms whose economic effects are felt daily, and this chapter keeps their uses and their damage clearly apart. It starts with the beneficial roles of bacteria — the nitrogen fixation that fertilises soil naturally, the dairy and food fermentations, the industrial production of antibiotics, enzymes and vitamins, and the decomposition that closes the nutrient cycle — then turns to the harmful side, where disease-causing bacteria and the spoiling of food account for almost all the damage. The final section treats the useful roles of fungi, from yeast in bread and brewing to mould-derived medicines and the partnership between fungi and plant roots.

learningOutcomes: Explain how Rhizobium and free-living bacteria add usable nitrogen to the soil.
Describe the bacterial processes used in dairy, food and industrial production.
List the major bacterial diseases with their causative organisms and modes of transmission.
Describe the useful roles of fungi in food, medicine, industry and plant nutrition.

learn.title: Useful bacteria in nature and industry

blocks.text: Bacteria matter most to agriculture because of nitrogen. Atmospheric nitrogen is unreactive and cannot be used directly by plants, and Rhizobium bacteria living in nodules on the roots of legumes such as pea, gram and groundnut have the enzyme nitrogenase that converts it into ammonia, which the plant can incorporate into amino acids and proteins. The arrangement is mutually beneficial: the plant supplies the bacteria with carbohydrates from photosynthesis and the bacteria supply fixed nitrogen, and the swollen nodules are the visible evidence of the partnership. Free-living bacteria such as Azotobacter and Clostridium fix nitrogen in the soil without any plant partner. Beyond nitrogen, bacteria are decomposers that break down dead plants, animals and animal waste, releasing carbon, nitrogen and minerals back into the soil in a form roots can absorb — without them, dead material would simply accumulate and the soil would be exhausted. In industry, Lactobacillus and Streptococcus convert lactose in milk to lactic acid, which sours the milk and sets it into curd, and related cultures ripen cheese. Acetobacter converts alcohol to acetic acid in vinegar production, while bacteria are also the source of antibiotics such as streptomycin and of industrial enzymes, vitamins and biogas.

blocks.caption: Useful activities of bacteria
rows: Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes
Nitrogen fixed in the soil without a host
Minerals returned to the soil; waste cleared
Pectin and soft tissues digested away
Secretions that kill or inhibit microbes
Bacterial rennet, vitamin B12, vitamin K

items: Rhizobium is a symbiotic bacterium, so the benefit runs both ways — sugar from the plant, fixed nitrogen from the bacterium.
The enzyme nitrogenase is what allows the conversion of nitrogen gas to ammonia, and it is inactivated by oxygen.
Root nodules in legumes let farmers rotate pulses with cereals to restore soil nitrogen naturally.
Saprophytic bacteria feed on dead matter, and their work is what gardeners call the soil being rich.
Curd formation is caused by lactic acid lowering the pH so that milk proteins coagulate.
Retting of jute and flax uses bacterial digestion of the soft tissue so the fibre can be peeled away.
Antibiotics are substances produced by one microorganism that inhibit or kill another, discovered originally from moulds and later from soil bacteria.
Bacteria in sewage treatment use the waste as food and convert it into less harmful, stable material.
Denitrifying bacteria are the exception that harms soil fertility by converting nitrates back to nitrogen gas.

items.text: A farmer sows soybean followed by wheat on the same field: the soybean's root nodules have added fixed nitrogen to the soil, so the wheat needs less applied fertiliser the following season.
items.note: This crop rotation is the practical economic value of Rhizobium.

items.text: In a biogas plant, anaerobic bacteria digest cattle dung and produce methane, which is then burned as fuel — decomposition put to direct commercial use.
items.note: The same decomposition that recycles nutrients can be captured for energy.

blocks.text: Pathogenic bacteria cause disease in two broad ways: by multiplying in a tissue and destroying it, or by releasing toxins that damage the body at a distance from the site of infection. Each bacterial disease is named after its causative organism, and learning the pair together is what makes answering straightforward. Tuberculosis attacks the lungs and is spread by droplets from an infected person coughing or sneezing, and it is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Cholera is an infection of the small intestine causing severe watery diarrhoea and rapid dehydration, spread through contaminated water and food, and caused by Vibrio cholerae. Typhoid fever is spread by contaminated food and water handled by a carrier and is caused by Salmonella typhi. Plague, historically the most destructive, is carried by fleas that live on rats and is caused by Yersinia pestis; the bacterium blocks the flea's gut so the starving flea bites repeatedly and spreads it. Diphtheria, tetanus, pneumonia and leprosy are further bacterial diseases, and dysentery is caused by Shigella. Non-pathogenic harms include the spoilage of stored food and the fouling of water pipes by iron-oxidising bacteria.

blocks.caption: Principal bacterial diseases
rows: Airborne droplets from coughing and sneezing
Bubonic form in lymph nodes; pneumonic form in lungs
Fleas from infected rats, then droplets
Spores entering a deep wound or burn
Droplets; often follows a viral infection

items: A disease-causing organism is called a pathogen, and a bacterium that carries a disease without suffering from it is a carrier.
Most bacterial diseases enter through the mouth in contaminated food or water, or through the lungs in droplets.
Boiling, pasteurisation and sterilisation kill vegetative bacterial cells, which is why they are used for food and instruments.
Cholera kills through dehydration rather than through tissue destruction, so replacement of fluid is the immediate treatment.
Tetanus and diphtheria are classic toxin-mediated diseases: the damage is done by a substance released by the bacterium.
Improving sanitation, protecting food and water supplies and isolating patients all interrupt the route of transmission.
Antibiotics work against bacteria but not against viruses, which is why they are useless against the common cold.
Storage of food in a cool, dry, sealed condition slows bacterial multiplication and so prevents spoilage.

items.text: A cut from a rusty nail carries Clostridium tetani spores deep into tissue, where the absence of oxygen lets them germinate and release the toxin that causes lockjaw.
items.note: The wound matters because the spores are anaerobic — the depth, not the rust itself, is decisive.

items.text: Water treatment with filtration and chlorination broke the transmission of cholera in city after city, showing that the control of water supply prevents the disease rather than treating it.
items.note: Prevention acts on the route, whereas treatment acts on the patient.

blocks.text: Yeast, a single-celled fungus, is the most economically important of the group because of fermentation. In bread making, yeast ferments the sugars in dough to ethanol and carbon dioxide, and it is the carbon dioxide that expands in the oven and raises the loaf — the ethanol mostly evaporates during baking. In brewing and wine making the same fermentation produces alcohol, which is then concentrated by distillation where a stronger spirit is required. Yeast is also grown as a protein-rich food supplement, sometimes called single-cell protein, because it reproduces rapidly and can be cultivated on industrial waste. Beyond yeast, moulds are used to produce medicines: Penicillium yields penicillin, the first antibiotic, and other fungi yield griseofulvin and statins. Certain fungi are used in the manufacture of organic acids, such as citric acid from Aspergillus niger, and in the production of enzymes used in food processing. Edible fungi such as the mushroom and the morel are cultivated as food. Finally, mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association between a fungus and the roots of a plant, in which the fungal hyphae spread far into the soil and absorb water and mineral salts far more effectively than the root could alone, while the plant supplies the fungus with carbohydrates.

blocks.caption: Useful roles of fungi
rows: Sugar fermented to ethanol and carbon dioxide
Secretion of penicillin, which inhibits bacteria
Fermentation yielding citric and gluconic acids
Cultivated and harvested as edible fungi
Hyphae extend the root's absorbing area
Improved uptake of water and minerals
Fungi and algae together are sensitive to sulphur dioxide

items: Yeast is used in bread because of the carbon dioxide it produces, and in brewing because of the ethanol — one organism, two products.
Bread dough is sometimes left to stand so that the yeast can act before the heat of the oven kills it and sets the structure.
Penicillium was found to inhibit staphylococci on a culture plate, which is how the first antibiotic came to be discovered.
Antibiotics from moulds act by disrupting bacterial cell walls or protein synthesis, and they have no effect on viruses.
Mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of a fungus, cultivated on composted material rather than in sunlight, so they need no chlorophyll.
Mycorrhizal fungi are essential to many trees: without them, the roots absorb far fewer minerals and the seedling struggles.
Yeasts and moulds need no light and no chlorophyll, which is why fungi are placed with animals rather than plants in their nutrition.
Fungal fermentation is carried out in controlled vessels so that temperature, pH and oxygen can be maintained at their optimum.

items.text: A baker adds a pinch of yeast to warm dough with a little sugar; after an hour the dough has doubled in size because fermentation has released carbon dioxide that becomes trapped in the gluten network.
items.note: The temperature matters — too hot kills the yeast, too cold slows it almost to a stop.

items.text: A forester dusts tree seedlings with mycorrhizal fungus before planting them out, because the fungal hyphae explore a volume of soil that the young root could never reach on its own.
items.note: The association benefits the fungus too, which receives sugars from the seedling.

learn.title: Putting bacteria and fungi side by side

blocks.text: Many exam questions require bacteria and fungi to be contrasted directly, so the structural difference must be precise. Bacteria are prokaryotic, with no membrane-bound nucleus and no organelles such as mitochondria, a cell wall usually made of peptidoglycan, and reproduction by simple binary fission. Fungi are eukaryotic, with a true nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall of chitin, and most reproduce by spore formation, sexually or asexually. Both are absorptive in nutrition — they secrete enzymes onto their food and take up the products — and both are largely saprophytic, which is why both are essential decomposers. The distinction matters economically: an antibiotic that disrupts bacterial cell wall synthesis has no effect on a fungus, because a chitin wall is built differently, and conversely an antifungal will not treat a bacterial infection. Naming the organism, the process and the product is the reliable structure for any economic-importance answer, since credit is given for all three.

blocks.caption: Bacteria against fungi
rows: Single cells, cocci, bacilli or spirilla
Unicellular yeasts or branching filaments called hyphae
Mainly by spores, sexual or asexual
Single circular chromosome in a nucleoid
Sensitive to antibiotics such as streptomycin
Not affected by antibiotics; needs an antifungal

items: Both groups are absorptive feeders and both are the principal decomposers of dead organic matter.
A fungus differs from a bacterium chiefly in being eukaryotic and in having a chitin wall rather than a peptidoglycan one.
Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as the peptidoglycan wall, which is why they do not act on fungal infections.
A yeast is a unicellular fungus, while a mould is made of branching hyphae — a difference of form, not of kingdom.
The hyphae of a mould give an enormous surface area, which is what makes fungal absorption so efficient.
Both bacteria and fungi are used industrially, but the products differ: bacteria give streptomycin, fungi give penicillin.
Nitrogen fixation is a bacterial achievement; fungi do not fix atmospheric nitrogen.
Naming the organism, the process and the product is the structure that earns full credit in economic-importance answers.

items.text: A patient with a fungal skin infection is given an antifungal rather than penicillin, because penicillin acts on peptidoglycan synthesis and a chitin-walled fungus has no such target.
items.note: The structural difference directly explains why the medicines differ.

items.text: Wheat straw buried in damp soil disappears within a season as bacteria and fungi secrete enzymes onto it and absorb the products, returning the minerals to the soil for the next crop.
items.note: This is the economic role that underlies all the others — nothing is lost from the cycle.

figures.caption: Figure: Nitrogen fixation in a legume root nodule
figures.description: A legume root drawn in longitudinal section showing several rounded swellings, the root nodules, cut open to reveal a mass of bacteria-containing tissue inside. An arrow series shows atmospheric nitrogen entering the nodule and being converted to ammonia, which is passed into the root and up to the leaves, while an arrow of carbohydrates runs from the leaves down to the nodule to feed the bacteria. The nodule is shown supplied with its own blood vessels branching from the root's vascular tissue.

figures.caption: Figure: Yeast fermentation in bread dough
figures.description: A three-stage sequence. First, a bowl of dough with yeast cells drawn budding and sugar present. Second, the same dough with arrows of carbon dioxide forming bubbles trapped in the gluten network, and ethanol marked as evaporating. Third, the baked loaf with a risen crumb full of set bubbles, the yeast shown killed by the heat of the oven, and a caption noting that the carbon dioxide did the raising.

figures.caption: Figure: Mycorrhiza around a plant root
figures.description: A plant root in cross-section with a dense sheath of fungal hyphae wrapping it, and long hyphae radiating far out into the soil beyond the zone the root hairs could reach. Two opposing arrows show the exchange: mineral salts and water travelling inward along the hyphae to the root, and sugars from the plant's photosynthesis travelling outward to the fungal hyphae.

keyPoints: Rhizobium lives in legume root nodules and converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia the plant can use.
Azotobacter and Clostridium fix nitrogen in the soil without needing a plant host.
Saprophytic bacteria and fungi decompose dead matter and return minerals to the soil.
Lactobacillus ferments lactose to lactic acid, which sets milk into curd and ripens cheese.
Bacteria are used to produce antibiotics such as streptomycin, as well as industrial enzymes and vitamins.
Bacterial diseases are named for their causative organism: tuberculosis by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, cholera by Vibrio cholerae, typhoid by Salmonella typhi.
Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated food and water; tuberculosis spreads in airborne droplets.
Yeast raises bread by releasing carbon dioxide during fermentation and produces alcohol in brewing.
Penicillium is the source of penicillin, the first antibiotic, and Aspergillus niger yields citric acid.
Mycorrhiza is a fungal-plant partnership in which the hyphae greatly extend the root's absorbing reach.
Bacteria are prokaryotic with a peptidoglycan wall; fungi are eukaryotic with a chitin wall, which is why antibiotics do not work on fungi.
examFocus: An economic-importance answer earns credit for three things together — the organism, the process, and the product or result — so give all three for every use.
For each bacterial disease give the causative organism as well as the mode of transmission; naming the disease alone is rarely the whole question.
Never credit antibiotics with curing viral infections, and never describe them as working against fungi, whose chitin wall is a different target.
In the bacteria against fungi contrast, the prokaryote against eukaryote distinction is the primary point; the wall material is the second.
State the benefit of nitrogen fixation to the plant and to the farmer separately when asked about economic importance.

vocabulary.meaning: Conversion of atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia usable by plants.
Symbiotic bacterium living in the root nodules of legumes and fixing nitrogen.
Organism that feeds on dead and decaying organic matter by external digestion.
Anaerobic breakdown of sugar by a microorganism to give alcohol, acid or gas.
Substance produced by a microorganism that kills or inhibits another microorganism.
Symbiotic association between fungal hyphae and a plant root.
Sugar-and-amino-acid polymer that stiffens a bacterial cell wall.

questions.prompt: Which bacterium fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants?
questions.explanation: Rhizobium lives symbiotically inside the root nodules of legumes such as pea, gram and groundnut, where the enzyme nitrogenase converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia that the plant can use to build proteins. Lactobacillus sours milk, Vibrio cholerae causes cholera, and Penicillium is a mould rather than a bacterium.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing Penicillium because it is famous for a useful product. It is a fungus, and it makes penicillin rather than fixing nitrogen.

questions.prompt: The bacterium that causes cholera is __________, while the bacterium that causes tuberculosis is __________.
questions.explanation: Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae, a curved rod that infects the small intestine and is carried in contaminated water, producing the toxin that causes severe watery diarrhoea. Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which attacks the lungs and spreads in the droplets produced by coughing and sneezing.
questions.commonMistake: Writing the disease name as the organism name. Diseases and pathogens are asked as a pair, so the binomial form matters.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a useful activity of bacteria with the organism responsible?
questions.explanation: Streptomyces is a soil bacterium that produces streptomycin and related antibiotics, and it is a genuine bacterial contribution to medicine. Bread rising is done by yeast, which is a fungus, curd formation by Lactobacillus rather than Rhizobium, and penicillin comes from the mould Penicillium, not from Acetobacter which makes vinegar.
questions.commonMistake: Pairing penicillin with a bacterium because antibiotics are associated with bacteria. Penicillin itself comes from a mould.

questions.prompt: Explain the mutual benefit that results from the association between Rhizobium and a leguminous plant.
questions.answer: The plant provides the bacterium with a protected place to live inside the root nodule and supplies it with carbohydrates produced during photosynthesis, which the bacterium uses as an energy source. In return, the bacterium uses the enzyme nitrogenase to convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which the plant incorporates into amino acids and proteins that it could not otherwise make. Both partners therefore gain something they cannot obtain efficiently on their own, which is why the arrangement is described as mutually beneficial or symbiotic.
questions.explanation: Both directions of the exchange must be given, since the benefit is mutual by definition: carbohydrate from plant to bacterium, fixed nitrogen from bacterium to plant. Describing only the plant's gain describes parasitism or a one-sided service rather than symbiosis.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the plant gives the bacterium oxygen. Nitrogenase is inactivated by oxygen, and the nodule actually keeps oxygen tension low to protect it.

questions.prompt: Describe how bacteria cause harm to human beings and to stored food, giving specific examples of each.
questions.answer: In human disease, pathogenic bacteria either multiply in a tissue and destroy it or release toxins that damage the body elsewhere. Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is contracted when droplets from an infected person's cough are inhaled and the bacteria multiply in the lungs, destroying lung tissue and impairing gas exchange. Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae, is swallowed in contaminated water; the bacterium multiplies in the small intestine and releases a toxin that drives a massive loss of fluid, so the danger is dehydration rather than destruction of tissue. Tetanus, caused by Clostridium tetani, enters through a deep wound and releases a toxin that acts on nerves, producing painful muscular spasms. In stored food, bacteria contaminate the surface and, in warm and moist conditions, multiply rapidly and secrete enzymes that break down proteins, fats and sugars, producing off flavours, unpleasant odours and sometimes harmful toxins — which is why food is preserved by cooling, drying, salting or sealing it.
questions.explanation: The question asks for two categories with examples of each, so both the disease group and the food group must be covered. Three named diseases with their organisms satisfy the first, and the mechanism of spoilage with the reason preservation methods work satisfies the second.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only diseases. The food-spoilage half of the question carries its own marks and is easily forgotten once the disease list begins.

questions.prompt: A farmer grows a pulse crop and then plants a cereal on the same land the following season, expecting to use less fertiliser. Which economic role of bacteria explains this?
options: Nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium in root nodules
Production of antibiotics that suppress crop disease
Fermentation of sugars in the soil
questions.answer: Nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium in root nodules
questions.explanation: The pulse crop's root nodules house Rhizobium, which converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia and enriches the soil with usable nitrogen compounds. When the cereal is planted afterwards, it can use that stored nitrogen, so less artificial fertiliser is needed. Decomposition recycles nitrogen already present but does not add any, and the other options do not act as fertiliser.
questions.commonMistake: Selecting decomposition, which returns minerals but does not introduce new nitrogen into the system.

questions.prompt: Explain why an antibiotic prescribed for a bacterial infection will not treat a fungal infection, referring to the structural difference between the two organisms. State what kind of organism causes the common cold and why antibiotics are useless against it.
questions.answer: Antibiotics act on structures or processes that bacteria possess and fungi do not. Penicillin, for example, blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall, so the growing bacterium bursts; streptomycin binds to bacterial ribosomes and disrupts protein synthesis. A fungal cell is eukaryotic, with a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes of the larger eukaryotic type, and its cell wall is built of chitin rather than peptidoglycan. Since the antibiotic's target is absent from a fungus, the drug has nothing to act on and the infection continues. A fungal infection therefore requires an antifungal, which acts on chitin synthesis or on fungal membrane sterols such as ergosterol. The common cold is caused by a virus, not a bacterium or a fungus. A virus has no metabolism of its own and no cell wall; it simply hijacks the machinery of the host's own cells to reproduce. Antibiotics are designed to attack bacterial structures, so there is no target for them in a virus, and taking them for a cold does nothing to shorten the illness while it does expose the body's bacteria to selective pressure.
questions.explanation: The first half must identify the antibiotic's target and show it is missing from a fungus, which is an argument from structure. The second half must name the virus as the cause and explain that a virus has no independent metabolism or bacterial structures to attack, which is why antibiotics are ineffective.
questions.commonMistake: Saying antibiotics do not work on viruses because viruses are not alive. The real reason is that the drug's target structures are not present in a virus.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of yeast in bread making.
questions.answer: Yeast is added to flour dough containing a little sugar, and it carries out anaerobic fermentation, converting the sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide is released as bubbles that become trapped in the elastic gluten network of the dough, so the dough expands and doubles in size. When the dough is baked the trapped gas expands further and the structure sets, giving the loaf its light, open texture; the ethanol formed evaporates during baking, leaving no taste of alcohol.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify which of the two fermentation products does the work — the carbon dioxide, not the ethanol — and explain how the gas is retained, since bubbles escaping would leave the loaf flat. Mentioning that the ethanol evaporates completes the account.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the yeast makes the dough rise by fermenting to alcohol. Alcohol is a liquid and would not raise the loaf; the gas does.

questions.prompt: Which useful role of fungi is shown by the association between fungal hyphae and the roots of a forest tree?
options: Mycorrhiza, which extends the root's absorption of water and minerals
Decomposition of the tree's own roots
questions.answer: Mycorrhiza, which extends the root's absorption of water and minerals
questions.explanation: Mycorrhiza is a symbiotic partnership in which fungal hyphae surround and penetrate the root and spread far into the soil, absorbing water and mineral salts far beyond the reach of the root hairs and passing them to the plant. The plant supplies the fungus with carbohydrates from photosynthesis. Fermentation belongs to yeast, penicillin to Penicillium, and decomposition is not an association with a living root.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing decomposition because fungi are decomposers. Mycorrhiza is a living partnership with a healthy root, not decay.

questions.prompt: The antibiotic penicillin is obtained from the mould __________, while the raising of bread dough is brought about by the carbon dioxide released during fermentation by __________.
questions.explanation: Penicillin was first isolated from Penicillium notatum, a fungus that secretes the substance to inhibit competing bacteria, and it remains the model for antibiotic production. Bread is raised by yeast, typically Saccharomyces, whose fermentation of the sugars in the dough releases the carbon dioxide that becomes trapped and expands the loaf during proving and baking.
questions.commonMistake: Naming a bacterium as the source of penicillin because antibiotics are so closely associated with bacteria. Penicillin comes from a mould.

questions.prompt: A village draws its drinking water from an open well that is also used to wash clothes and dispose of kitchen waste. Explain the health risk this presents, name two bacterial diseases likely to arise, and describe two measures that would reduce the risk.
questions.answer: Washing and kitchen waste introduce faecal and organic matter into the well, and any person with a bacterial infection who uses the well contaminates it further. Cholera, typhoid and dysentery are transmitted by the faecal-oral route: organisms shed in the waste multiply in the water, are swallowed in drinking water or on food washed in it, and then infect the intestine of the person who drinks it. Two diseases likely to arise are cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae, and typhoid, caused by Salmonella typhi; both produce severe illness and both spread rapidly through a community sharing one water source. Two measures that would reduce the risk are, first, to prevent contamination at the source by lining and covering the well, moving washing and waste disposal away from it, and installing a hand pump so that no bucket is dipped in. Second, to treat the water before drinking, by boiling it or filtering and chlorinating it, which kills or removes the bacteria and breaks the transmission cycle.
questions.explanation: The reasoning must trace the faecal-oral route from the contamination to the infection, since that is what makes the risk real rather than merely unpleasant. Two diseases with their organisms and two different measures — one preventing entry and one treating the water — together cover all four marks.
questions.commonMistake: Suggesting only boiling the water while leaving the well contaminated. The question asks for two measures, and a source-side control is the more durable of the two.
